posts.title: AI agents are arriving everywhere, and landing on the cancel list
posts.summary: Gartner expects agents in 40% of enterprise apps by the end of 2026 and predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by 2027. Both can be true.
body: Gartner expects up to 40% of enterprise applications to include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from under 5% in 2025. The same firm predicts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing rising costs, unclear business value and weak risk controls.

Both forecasts can be true at once. Agents are showing up inside the software teams already use, while many custom agent projects started on hype will stall. Gartner also warns about "agent washing": by its estimate, only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI offer real agentic capabilities.

From a delivery seat, the pattern is familiar. The projects that survive pick a narrow task with a measured baseline, budget for evaluation and guardrails from day one, and name who approves what the agent does. Projects that start with "let's add an agent" and no success metric are the ones that end up cut.
My takeaway: before funding an agent, write down the decision it supports, the metric it should move, and the control that stops it when it is wrong.

posts.title: AI agents are getting authority faster than they are getting oversight
posts.summary: New surveys show agents approving transactions and changing controls while only 9% of firms have redesigned workflows and 5% of automakers report mature AI governance.
body: Optro surveyed 417 governance, risk, compliance, audit and security leaders at organizations with 250 or more employees in North America and Europe. 38% let AI agents approve or reject transactions, 34% let them modify controls or policies, and 27% let them change user permissions or access rights. Meanwhile, 34% have acted on an inaccurate agent decision or output, 30% have seen an agent take an unintended action, and only 9% have redesigned workflows to accommodate agents.

A Capgemini Research Institute survey of 800 automotive executives shows the same gap in one industry. 68% already use (33%) or pilot (35%) agentic AI in product development, but only 5% report fully mature AI governance. Trust reaches 59% for upstream research and concept work and falls to 40% in development activities.

From a delivery seat, adoption is no longer the bottleneck; oversight is. Optro also found 46% of organizations say employees now spend more time reviewing, validating or correcting AI outputs. That is the hidden cost of dropping an agent into an old workflow instead of redesigning the workflow around it. I treat agent permissions the way I treat privileged access: scoped, logged and reviewed on a schedule.
My takeaway: before an agent can approve, change or grant anything, give that authority a named human owner, an audit trail and a rollback path. If you cannot, keep the agent in recommend-only mode.

posts.title: AI agents need an ID badge and a manager
posts.summary: ServiceNow's AI Passport gives agents a signed runtime credential, and one CISO says every one of his 1,500 agents has an employee ID and a manager.
body: On October 15, ServiceNow announced AI Passport, a cryptographically signed credential that AI agents check at runtime to verify the scope an enterprise has authorized. It applies to ServiceNow and third-party agents and to MCP servers, and it can redirect, restrict or terminate an agent that drifts. It ships with shadow AI detection and 400+ discovery connectors, and is expected in Q4 2026.

The announcement included two numbers worth noting. ServiceNow's 2026 Banking AI Maturity Index found that 100 percent of banks report using AI, but only 24 percent have the governance to match it. And the CISO of LTM said the company has deployed 1,500 AI agents, each assigned an employee ID and manager.

From a delivery seat, that second detail matters more than the product. Once you have dozens of agents across teams and vendors, the hard question is no longer what an agent can do. It is which agent did it, under whose authority, and who answers for it. Identity is how you get there, and it is far easier to design in at the pilot than to retrofit after go-live.
My takeaway: register every agent like a new hire before it touches production. Give it a unique identity, a named human manager, a defined scope and an offboarding date.
